source.title: On Batching Variable Size Inputs for Training End-to-End Speech Enhancement Systems
source.authors: Philippe Gonzalez; Tommy Sonne Alstrøm; T. May

record.file_problem: The supplied text contains the full paper. The table is flattened, but the prose describes its main trends.
record.tranche_reason: Tests the effect of batch size on held-out speech-enhancement performance in a new modality, using matched and mismatched evaluation conditions.
record.gate_note: The paper reports results for batch sizes and batching strategies. Its prose states that ΔESTOI and ΔSNR decrease with larger batch sizes across all three strategies, with a stronger trend in mismatched conditions; ΔPESQ has no particular trend. The study does not report training error, so it does not directly measure a train–test gap.
record.test_reason: The study measures batch-size effects on speech enhancement, whereas V5 names image classifiers and language models. Conv-TasNet predicts enhanced waveforms, and its PESQ, ESTOI and SNR scores do not measure either named task. The findings motivate a broader claim but do not directly test a supplied version.
record.authors_conclusion: The record accurately paraphrases the authors: smaller batches improve speech-enhancement performance, especially in mismatched conditions, while sorted or bucket batching reduces padding and training time with similar performance. Their broad performance statement should be read alongside the reported absence of a PESQ trend. Dynamic batching also reduces allocated GPU memory at comparable training times.
record.recipe_differences: Speech enhancement with variable-length noisy and reverberant audio; evaluates batch-size and batching-strategy effects rather than image or language classification.
record.method_sensitivity: Batch size affects ΔESTOI and ΔSNR; the trend is significantly stronger in mismatched conditions. No particular ΔPESQ trend is observed. Batching strategy affects padding and training time, while sorted batching is reported to have similar performance to random batching.

fits_no_version.finding: With 150 training epochs and Adam at learning rate 0.001, larger dynamic batches generally reduce ESTOI and SNR improvements across random, sorted and bucket batching; the trend is stronger under distribution mismatch. For random batching, increasing the dynamic batch from 2 to 128 seconds reduces mismatched SNR improvement from 4.14 ± 0.03 to 3.40 ± 0.02. Small dynamic batches also change input segmentation.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Larger batches can reduce held-out speech-enhancement performance under a fixed epoch budget, with effects depending on evaluation distribution and input segmentation.

fits_no_version.finding: The authors report no particular PESQ trend with dynamic batch size in matched or mismatched evaluation.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Batch-size effects in speech enhancement depend on the evaluation metric; intelligibility and signal-fidelity trends need not appear in perceptual-quality scores.

record.peer_reviewed: IEEE International Conference on Acoustics, Speech, and Signal Processing
record.problems: The study reports held-out speech-enhancement metrics rather than training error, so it does not measure the train–test gap directly. The supplied prose does not state exact Figure 4 values.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows extracted. Table 1 reports results for many individual batch-size and strategy combinations, but the supplied table is flattened and the prose summarizes the relevant performance trend across strategies; Figure 4 values are figure-only in the supplied text.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and natural-label held-out accuracy.
Width increases beyond zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers.
Batch-size effects in image classifiers and language models, including recovery through longer training or adapted recipes.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its association with generalization gaps.
Removing memorized examples versus random examples.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source. No training-error measurement is required to assess V5's held-out-performance prediction; the decisive mismatch here is the task scope. Stronger degradation under mismatch would not itself limit a batch-size penalty claim.

versions.untested_parts: Width sweep beyond the interpolation threshold.
Training-versus-test error gaps; language models; alternative training durations and adapted recipes such as learning-rate scaling with warmup.
Sharpness and other measured properties as predictors of the generalization gap.
Removing memorized training examples and measuring the resulting test-accuracy change.
